en: The Scripture on Protecting the State Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmaśrī, Imperially Appointed Court Attendant of the Third Rank,
Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of Enlightened Teaching, under Imperial Edict.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Blessed One was staying at the city of Kuru; traveling through the land to bring benefit and aid, he gradually arrived at the village of Tora and settled there with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, there were brahmins and great householders in that village who discussed among themselves, saying:
"This Great Śramaṇa Gautama has renounced his royal throne to leave the home life for the path;

his fruit is fulfilled and perfectly luminous, and his fame is heard everywhere. He is indeed the Worthy One, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One, the One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, the Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed One, the Tamer of Men, the Teacher of Gods and Humans, the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

Within the realms of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, and non-humans, having attained perfect enlightenment through his own practice and vows, he radiates great compassion and proclaims the True Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; profound in its words and meaning, pure and unadulterated, fully endowed with the characteristics of the complete and perfect holy life (brahmacarya).

Thus, being endowed with the most honored and supreme [qualities], we shall obtain great benefit if we behold him; therefore, we shall go to where the Buddha is to gaze upon him, pay homage, and offer praise.
Having deliberated together, the assembly went as one to the Buddha’s gathering.

Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, some prostrated before the Buddha, some merely joined their palms, and some offered various praises. Once this multitude had finished their prostrations and praises, they each sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for the assembly, causing their hearts to rejoice and inspiring them to resolve upon the Great Way.

Having heard and received the teaching, those brahmins, great elders, and others were all filled with joy and resolved upon the mind of the Great Way; they immediately rose from their seats, joined their palms toward the Buddha, praised him in various ways, paid homage to the Buddha, and withdrew.
At that time, there was a great elder in the assembly named Rāṣṭrapāla. Out of longing for the Buddha, he did not leave the dharma assembly and thought to himself:
"The Dharma I have heard is worthy of reliance; I shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment."
"If I remain at home, I shall dwell forever in saṃsāra. A Buddha is difficult to encounter;

therefore, out of faith, I have gone forth seeking liberation. For this reason, I now abandon all negligence and arouse great diligence. Relying on the Buddha, I have gone forth to purely cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya). I vow to shave off my hair and beard and don the dharma robes."

At that time, after the householder Rāṣṭrapāla had formed this thought, he rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying:

“Having heard the True Dharma from the World-Honored One, I have grown weary of the suffering of saṃsāra and have given rise to a mind of faith and joy; therefore, I now seek ordination from the Buddha.”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will accept me.
The Buddha said to Guhṇapāla, “You have left home out of faith; have your parents given their permission?”
Rāṣṭrapāla replied: “No, World-Honored One.”
"The parents will not permit it.
The Buddha said to Huguo:
"If your parents do not permit it, you may not go forth into homelessness."
Rāṣṭrapāla addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although my parents have not yet granted permission, I shall entreat them so that they will firmly grant their consent.”
The Buddha told Rakṣita:
"Just as you have wished, now is the very time.
At that moment, the elder Rakṣita, having received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew. Returning to his home, he spoke to his parents, saying:
"Parents, look upon me with compassion and grant me your permission to speak.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching at his assembly, I have fully understood all that I heard; I have given rise to right faith and desire to leave the household life."
"I only pray that my parents will grant me permission.
At that time, his parents said to Rāṣṭrapāla,
"If you delight in leaving the household life, what benefit do you seek?"
Furthermore, for what reason do you seek to leave the household life?
If you were to leave the household life, would you not have to live by begging for alms?

You should know that I now possess immeasurable wealth, treasures, and precious goods; you need only remain at home, relinquish your wealth to cultivate merit, and enjoy prosperity and happiness—why must you leave the household life?
Thus did his parents exhort him with kind words.
At that time, Rāṣṭrapāla spoke again, saying:
"Parents, please consider this: I am weary of saṃsāra and have renounced worldly glory; my resolve is to seek the life of a renunciant. I only pray that you will grant me your permission."
Thus did Rāṣṭrapāla entreat them repeatedly.
At that time, his parents spoke to him again:
"Since you are so firm in your resolve to seek renunciation, do not live by begging for alms?"

"My household possesses vast and immeasurable stores of gold, silver, and precious jewels; you need only remain at home, renounce your wealth to cultivate merit, and you shall enjoy prosperity and happiness—why must you leave the household life?"
Thus his parents entreated and exhorted him two or three times.
At that moment, Rāṣṭrapāla spoke again, saying:
"If my parents do not grant me permission, from this day forward I vow never to eat or drink until the end of my life."
Having made this vow, he immediately ceased all food and drink.
At that time, many kinsmen and acquaintances of the elder Guardian of the Nation, having heard of these events, went together to the residence of the elder’s parents and addressed them, saying:
"O Elder Master!..."
"We have all heard that your son Rāṣṭrapāla delights in renunciation; although he seeks it with resolve, you do not grant him permission.
We know your son well: though he enjoys wealth and pleasure, his aspiration for the Path is firm.
If you do not grant him permission now, he will instead suffer grief and distress until the end of his life, and this will cause you to experience the suffering of separation from those you love."
"Therefore, you all should grant permission for him to go forth as a monk.
At that time, the head of the household, seeing that his son’s friends were earnestly entreating him, immediately granted permission for him to go forth.
At that time, many of Rāṣṭrapāla’s acquaintances, having received his father’s instructions, went to Rāṣṭrapāla and said to him together:
"Rāṣṭrapāla, you should know that your parents have now granted you permission to go forth."

At that time, Rāṣṭrapāla, having received his parents' instructions, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He immediately went to his parents, paid his respects and took his leave, then returned to the place where the Buddha was.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s presence, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Now that my parents have already granted me permission to leave the household life,
I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will graciously accept me and ordain me as a bhikṣu.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāṣṭrapāla, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!
Now is precisely the right time; I shall accept you.

At that moment, Rāṣṭrapāla’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and he was clothed in the saṃghāṭī robe, assuming the appearance of a bhikṣu. He practiced the holy life (brahmacarya), abandoning negligence and departing from all sorrow and affliction. His mind became naturally disciplined and supple, and he realized the purity of the Dharma, attaining the realization: “Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.”
At that time, after the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla had attained the destruction of the outflows, he remained in dependence upon the Buddha for ten years.

Having completed those ten years, he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and approached the place where the Buddha was; prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and joining his palms to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"In my former life, I resided in the village of Tora; I renounced all my kinsmen and left the household life out of faith.
Now, as I reflect, I wish to return to my native place to be near my relatives, and I await the Buddha’s instruction."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the inclinations of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla’s mind and observing that his resolve was firm and his desire to bring extensive benefit [to beings], and considering further that while formerly at home he had always remained detached from all desires—having thus observed him, he addressed him, saying:
“Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla!”
"Now is precisely the right time; you may act according to your own intention.

At that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, having received the Buddha’s instruction, was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and withdrew. He returned to his native place, traveling through the intermediate stages until he reached his original village.
When the night had passed, at the hour of the morning, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and went for alms from house to house until he reached his own dwelling.
There he saw a woman outside the door of her house holding a full vessel of food that she was about to throw away. Seeing this, the Venerable said to the woman:
"You have no sense of shame; do not discard this food."
"How could it be otherwise than if you were to give me this food and place it in my bowl, whereby you would surely obtain benefit?
At that time, having heard the Venerable One's words, the woman felt a sense of deep reverence; she immediately gave him the food and placed it in his bowl.
Having accepted it, the Venerable One went beneath a great tree, spread out his seat, and sat down intending to eat.
At that time, the woman who had been before him thought to herself:
"This is my master, the Venerable Guardian of the Nation."
At that time, having formed this thought, the woman went to the householder’s master and said to him:
"Just now, outside the gate, I saw the householder’s son holding an alms-bowl and begging for food; he went beneath a great tree, spread out a seat, and intended to eat."
When the elder heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately asked the woman:
"Is what you have said true?"
The woman replied, "It is indeed so.
At that time, the elder quickly left his own house and went beneath the great tree; having arrived there, he saw in truth that Guṇapāla was there intending to eat, and he immediately said to him:
"My son, Guardian of the Nation!
Having left your own home to travel abroad and having passed through such experiences, you have now arrived at this village yet do not enter your own house; what does this mean?"
Then that Guardian of the Nation replied to his father, saying:
"Such is the ritual of our śramaṇa dharma; it is not appropriate for me to enter another's house."
Then the elder, supporting Rāṣṭrapāla, returned to his own home; having arrived at the house, he prepared a seat and invited him to sit.
At that time, Rāṣṭrapāla’s mother approached her son, and with a heart of intense affection, she comforted him repeatedly and said to Rāṣṭrapāla:
"My son, why have you so firmly resolved to leave the household life?"
"What benefit do you find now in this renunciation?
What have you gained?
You are merely seeking alms to sustain your life; therefore, you should no longer leave home, but rather give away your wealth to cultivate merit and enjoy the pleasures of abundance."

At that time, his compassionate mother employed various skillful means, feeling such deep attachment to her son that she could not bear to part from him. She further piled gold, silver, and all kinds of precious jewels before the Venerable One and said to her son:
"My son, you should know that I possess vast wealth and treasures which I now give to you; how much more so the father’s immeasurable wealth! For this reason, how can you leave the household life?"
"You are currently living as a householder; by renouncing wealth to perform meritorious deeds, you shall enjoy various riches and pleasures.
At that time, the Venerable One said to his mother:
"O compassionate mother, you should bear in mind that this much gold, silver, and various kinds of wealth and treasures are the root of all faults."
Having spoken these words, he loaded it onto a cart and carried it away to cast it into the river. He then addressed his mother again, saying:

"Compassionate Mother, you should reflect that such wealth and treasures, due to the attachment of greed, become the cause for the arising of various faults and lead to calamities—namely, the misfortunes of water, fire, kings, thieves, and wicked sons. Such various forms of suffering resulting from ruin arise; understand that this cause of suffering does not come from your mother."
At that time, the mother of Rāṣṭrapāla, unable to bear the thought of parting from her son, again devised a skillful means and thought to herself:
"I shall have his former wives, when he lived at home, adorned with ornaments of precious jewels upon their bodies, and bring them to Rāṣṭrapāla’s presence so as to please his heart."
Having had this thought, he went to his wife’s quarters and said to her:

“When your husband Rāṣṭrapāla was formerly at home, there were certain cherished jewels, necklaces, and ornaments that he delighted in; adorn yourself with them now and go to Rāṣṭrapāla to please his heart.”
Then, having received his command, the wife of Rāṣṭrapāla immediately adorned herself with various precious ornaments and went to where Rāṣṭrapāla was; arriving there, she said to him:
"O son of a householder!
"What do you think?
Is the holy life you maintain not for the sake of seeking celestial maidens? Rakṣita replied:
"No, sister! I maintain the practice of pure conduct (brahmacarya) in order to seek the fruit of the Way."
"What you have said is not correct.
At that time, when the wife of Rāṣṭrapāla heard the voice calling her "sister," she immediately changed her expression and withdrew in shame.
At that time, the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla thought to himself,
"The time for the meal is approaching," and he immediately said to his father:
“Householder! What food and drink do you have to offer me for my meal?
At that time, his parents personally presented various kinds of superior-flavored foods and drinks to offer to the Venerable One.

At that time, when the Venerable One had finished his meal, he washed his bowl, gathered his robes, arranged a seat, and sat down. He then expounded the True Dharma for his parents, causing them to give rise to joy and the aspiration for the Path. Furthermore, abiding in mid-air through his supernormal powers, he spoke this verse:
"Behold these painted forms and images, Adorned with various precious gems;
The deluded and confused are attached to them, But the wise always remain far removed."
"Craving is like a rope that can bind the world;
it deludes the foolish, while the wise always remain far removed from it.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the Venerable One descended from the air and returned to rest beneath the great tree.

At that time, there was a king named Kuru who, having mounted his carriage for an excursion outside, drew near to the vicinity of the village of Tora. An attendant minister addressed him, saying: "Great King!"
You should know that in this village there is a son of a householder named Rāṣṭrapāla; having abandoned his vast retinue and immeasurable wealth and treasures, he has gone forth into homelessness.
When the king heard this matter, he immediately asked the people of the village,
"Is it true that in this place there is the son of an elder named Rāṣṭrapāla, who has abandoned his kinsmen to go forth as a renunciant?"
Then the people of the village immediately reported to the king, saying: "Great King!
You should know that this matter is indeed so."
"The Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla constantly maintains the holy life beneath a great tree in our village; we, the people, draw near to him and make offerings.
Having heard this report, the king immediately went to that village and approached the place where the Venerable One was staying beneath the great tree.

At that time, the Venerable One observed from afar the approaching summons; seeing King Kuru hastening toward him, he immediately rose from his seat, stepped forward before the king, and spoke these words: "Great King!"
"Welcome! This realm is under the king's dominion; I now invite Your Majesty to go beneath that tree and take my seat.
Then the king replied:
“Rāṣṭrapāla! My intention is likewise; I wish to go to your place and take your seat.
Rāṣṭrapāla spoke again:
"Since the King's intention is thus, I have invited him.
At that time, the King, together with the Venerable One, went beneath a great tree and sat down upon a seat.
At that time, the Great King said to Guhāpati:
"There are four kinds of dharmas; it is by means of these four dharmas that one seeks to go forth from the household life.
What are these four dharmas?"
First, knowing one's relatives; second, knowing wealth and status; third, knowing illness; fourth, knowing old age—these are the four dharmas.
"What is meant by knowing one's relatives?"
That is to say, if there is a person whose vast circle of kinsmen suddenly disperses and perishes, that person reflects:
"My kinsmen, friends, and acquaintances have all dispersed and perished; I am now left all alone. I shall go forth into homelessness."
"This person sought to leave the household life because he understood that he had no relatives;
now you, Protector of the Nation!
have a vast circle of kin and are not alone, yet you do not understand what it means to leave the household life."
Furthermore, what is meant by "knowing wealth and nobility"?

It refers to a person who was previously very wealthy, possessing vast treasures, but later finds those resources exhausted and falls into poverty and suffering; because of this poverty, they form this thought:
Now, because of poverty, he forms this thought:
"I am currently suffering from poverty; I shall go forth into homelessness.
This person clearly understands that it is on account of poverty that he seeks to go forth.
Now, Rāṣṭrapāla! You possess immeasurable wealth and are not poor; how could you understand what it means to go forth?
Furthermore, how can one be said to know the suffering of illness?
It is said that if there is a person who has long lain ill with no one able to provide medical treatment, they form this thought:
"This illness of mine is deeply painful; therefore, I shall now seek to go forth into homelessness."
"This person understood that it is because of the suffering of illness that one seeks to leave the household life.
Now, you, Protector of the Nation!
You have little illness and little affliction, nor do you possess sorrow or pain; how then can you understand why one leaves the household life?"
Furthermore, what is meant by "knowing one's own decrepitude"?
It refers to when a person has reached advanced age and physical decline, and reflects thus:
"I am now old and decrepit; I can no longer benefit from worldly wealth and pleasures. Therefore, I should now seek to go forth into homelessness."
"This person, realizing that he was too decrepit to fulfill his duties, sought to leave the household life.
But now, you, Protector of the Nation!
You are in the prime of youth and vigor, and have not yet experienced the various pleasures; how can you understand what it means to leave the household life?"
Rāṣṭrapāla, having fulfilled these four dharmas, one may then go forth into homelessness.
Rāṣṭrapāla, I now ask you again: what have you seen or heard that led you to go forth?
At that time, the Venerable One replied to the king,
saying: "Great King,
you should know that there are four kinds of persons who seek to go forth into homelessness."
What are the four? They are aging, illness, craving, and death.

Transformation and decay that do not endure is called aging; the presence of disease and suffering without remedy is called illness; the lack of satiety is called craving; and the relinquishing and exhaustion of all objective spheres is called death.

"These four dharmas, our Buddha, the World-Honored One, has thoroughly understood and clearly perceived; I too have personally seen and heard them from the Buddha. For this reason, I have given rise to great faith and have gone forth into homelessness."
The King said: "Venerable One!
As previously explained in brief, I have not yet fully understood it. I only pray that the Venerable One will explain it to me in detail so that I may attain comprehension."
At that time, having heard the king’s words, the Venerable One said to him: “Great King,
most excellent!”
"As you wish, I shall explain it for you.
The king said, "Venerable One!"
"What is the meaning of 'aging' as the state of being subject to transformation and decay over time?
The Venerable One replied, "Great King!"
What do you think?
When a person reaches the age of twenty, thirty, or forty, what is the nature of their physical appearance, bodily strength, and their movements and conduct?
The king said, "Venerable One!

When a person reaches forty years from the age of twenty, they possess magnificent physical features; their bodily strength is robust and flourishing, and their movements are courageous and vigorous. In all their undertakings, they consider themselves to be without equal."
"When one reaches old age, being decrepit and past one's prime, one is no longer capable; the physical appearance changes, bodily strength becomes feeble, and one’s ability to move about declines.
The Venerable One replied, "As Your Majesty has said, this is the mark of aging that brings about transformation and decay in the world."
"Great King!
You should know that this is precisely what our Buddha calls the foremost dharma.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has thoroughly understood, thoroughly known, and skillfully expounded this dharma; I too have seen and heard it, and out of love for and aspiration toward this True Dharma, I have left the household life with faith."
Then that king said: "Venerable Protector of the Nation!
I too have encountered the True Dharma here with great fortune, and I cherish it and seek it with resolve."
Furthermore, the King said:
"Venerable Protector of the Nation!
Why is it that the presence of illness, characterized by suffering for which there is no remedy, is called the mark of disease?"
The Venerable One replied:
"Suppose there were a person who possessed great wealth and treasures, as well as immeasurable numbers of kinsmen and relatives.
What do you think?"
"If this person falls ill and undergoes various sufferings and afflictions, would his relatives and attendants also take those sufferings and afflictions upon themselves on his behalf?
The King replied, "No."
"Rāṣṭrapāla!
When a person lies ill, they alone must endure all manner of suffering; there is no one to take their place, nor is there any remedy.
The Venerable One replied:
"As Your Majesty has said, that there is no substitute and no rescue—this is the characteristic of illness; this is precisely the second Dharma taught by our Buddha.

Furthermore, the Blessed One thoroughly understands, thoroughly knows, and skillfully expounds this Dharma; I too have seen and heard it, and out of love for and aspiration toward this True Dharma, I have left the household life with faith."
Then that king said: "Venerable Protector of the Nation!
I too have encountered the True Dharma here with great fortune, and I cherish it and seek it with resolve."
The King asked again:
"Venerable One!
Why is it that being insatiable is called craving?"
The Venerable One replied:
"Great King, what do you think?"
The king is wealthy, and all the people residing within his domain—whether in the capital city or throughout the lands to the east, south, west, and north—are likewise all very rich.
The king said to the Venerable One, “So it is, so it is!
The Venerable One spoke again:
"Great King, the kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages over which you rule are so immensely wealthy that suppose there were someone who came by sea and said to the Great King:

'I have seen a certain country where the cities and towns are vast and the population is flourishing; its gold, silver, precious gems, and rare curiosities, as well as its elephants, horses, and military retinues, are immeasurable in number.'"
"Great King! Having heard this, what do you think?
The King said:
“Venerable Sir!
Having heard this matter, if I do not go there myself, I shall immediately dispatch an envoy to subdue them, bringing back precious treasures and various goods to further enrich my treasury.”
Then the Venerable One said: "Great King!
This lack of contentment is called craving; this is what the Buddha taught as the third dharma."

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has thoroughly understood, thoroughly known, and well-expounded this Dharma; I too have seen and heard it, and having found joy and aspiration for this True Dharma, I have left the home life with faith.
Then that king said: "Venerable Protector of the Nation!
I too have encountered this sublime Dharma with joy and love, and I am devotedly intent upon seeking it."
The King asked again:
"Venerable One!
How is it that abandoning all sensory objects is called death?"
The Venerable One replied:
"Great King, what do you think?"

Suppose I see a great treasure belonging to a very wealthy person; if that person were to depart from this world-system and be born in another world-system, would they be able to carry all those treasures with them?
The King said, “No. The Venerable One spoke again:
“Great King! In this world, to abandon all objects of affection and be born in another world—this is called death; this is the fourth dharma taught by the Buddha.”
"The Buddha has thoroughly understood and well-expounded this Dharma; I too have seen and heard it, and out of love for and aspiration toward this True Dharma, I have gone forth with faith.
The King said, "Venerable One!"
"I too have encountered this sublime Dharma with great fortune; I cherish it and seek it with resolve.
At that time, the Venerable One addressed the king again, saying:
"I wish to proclaim this meaning once more; you should listen well."
The King said: "Excellent! I am eager to hear it.
At that time, the Venerable One spoke these verses:
"I see people in the world who, out of craving and attachment, amass wealth;
because of that wealth they encounter hardships, yet their desires only increase further.
Kings rule over kingdoms and cities, vast and extending to the very shores of the ocean."
Thus, even without satiety, he further goes to invade other kingdoms.
All sentient beings in the world perish because of craving and attachment;
they give rise to grief and weep, crying out: "Alas! Why do you perish so quickly?"
Just as a person who has gathered wealth and treasures may, in turn, be consumed by fire,
so too do sentient beings follow their karma, receiving retribution for what they have done.
Wealth does not prolong life, nor can it prevent the onset of old age.
The rich and the poor are all extinguished; the honored and the young are all impermanent.
Illness does not choose between the brave and the strong, nor does it spare the honored or the young;
because of craving and attachment, none can escape impermanence.
Just as a person who commits theft In the end brings harm upon themselves, So too is the world perceived: One creates the causes of one's own evil.
As fruit falls of its own accord when ripe, So it is with the decay of the young and the old.
One performs actions with a joyful mind, yet receives retribution in suffering.
The foolish people of this world do not realize as they act;
when reborn in another life, they encounter suffering due to their hatred and attachment.
If one’s life should end within the womb, who could provide protection?
Even if one has close relatives and friends, once life has ended, how can they save one?
Desire can both destroy and bind; it increases the suffering of birth and all manner of fears.
"Seeing that the phenomena of the world are illusory, for this reason I have gone forth.
At that time, having heard the Venerable’s verses, King Kuru received them with joy and faith, and further said:
"Venerable Protector of the Nation, you are truly skilled in renunciation; therefore, I now take refuge in you."
Rāṣṭrapāla replied: "Great King! Do not take refuge in me;
it is in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha that I have taken refuge—Your Majesty should likewise take refuge in them."
The king said: "So it is, so it is!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and shall observe the precepts of an upāsaka for as long as I live."
At that time, having made his vow, the Great King paid homage to the Venerable One and returned to the royal palace.
From the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra*.
